query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy, the accelerated degradation under simultaneous high-temperature wear and corrosion is driven by a synergistic interaction at the phase boundaries; cyclic mechanical disruption (wear-induced rupture of protective oxide films) repeatedly exposes electrochemically dissimilar phases, triggering localized galvanic corrosion that in turn weakens the interphase bonding and enhances subsequent wear.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting distinct phases (e.g., a wear-resistant matrix and a corrosion-resistant secondary phase) with well-defined, heterogeneous phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Simultaneously subject the alloy to elevated-temperature wear and corrosive chemical environment, using in situ high-temperature tribocorrosion testing combined with real-time imaging and meso-scale simulations.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (to accelerate oxide film kinetics and chemical reactions), simultaneous mechanical loading (imparting wear) and exposure to a corrosive medium (e.g., saline solution), under controlled strain and temperature profiles that mimic service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfaces between dissimilar phases (e.g., between a harder, wear-resistant phase and a more chemically stable phase) where differences in electrochemical potential and mechanical response facilitate both film rupture and galvanic interactions.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, continuous wear leads to episodic rupture of the protective oxide films forming on phase surfaces. This exposes fresh, electrochemically dissimilar surfaces at the phase boundaries, resulting in localized galvanic corrosion. The corrosion accelerates material removal and promotes microcracking, which further enhances wear in a positive feedback loop.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline of isolated wear and isolated corrosion, the combined tribocorrosion process will show a total degradation rate that exceeds the arithmetic sum of individual processes. Specifically, both the wear volume loss and the corrosion current (or degradation depth) will be significantly higher in the coupled test, indicating synergistic degradation.
generation.baseline: The alloy’s degradation measured separately under pure wear conditions (in an inert or non-corrosive environment) and pure corrosion conditions (without mechanical loading) at the same elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: Results apply within the regime of elevated temperatures that accelerate oxide kinetics, under simultaneous application of wear stresses and corrosive chemical exposure. The hypothesis is constrained to eutectic high-entropy alloys having distinct phase boundaries with differential electrochemical and mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of oxide film rupture versus galvanic enhancement remain uncertain; additionally, the extent of microstructural damage may vary with phase morphology and distribution, which necessitates further systematic investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a set of controlled experiments where identical samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy are subjected to: (1) only elevated-temperature wear (in inert atmosphere), (2) only elevated-temperature corrosion (without mechanical loading), and (3) simultaneous elevated-temperature tribocorrosion. In situ high-temperature imaging and synchronized meso-scale simulations will be used to monitor oxide film behavior and microstructural damage in real time.
measurements: Wear volume loss via profilometry or mass loss measurements
Corrosion current density and/or depth of corrosion penetration
Real-time observations of oxide film rupture and repassivation cycles
Microstructural analysis of phase boundary integrity via SEM/EDS post-experiment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation observed under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions is equal to or less than the simple sum of the separate wear and corrosion degradation (i.e., no synergy is observed), or if there is no evidence of repeated oxide film rupture and localized galvanic attack at phase boundaries, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Conductive and wear performance of the NbMoTaW coatings on AFM probe tips
cited_evidence.text: In summary, this study has established a conductivity model for the HEA system Nb-Mo-Ta-W, designed alloy compositions with high conductivity and wear resistance, which can be applied to enhance the atomic-level resolution and lifespan of atomic force microscope probes. By adjusting the composition, a refractory high-entropy material of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 was endowed with both high hardness and electrical conductivity. We indicate that the conductivity of Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEAs can be modulated through the cocktail effect but tends to differ by an order of magnitude compared to linear combinations. The reasons for the decrease in conductivity are attributed to changes in the plasma frequency and relaxation time resulting from lattice distortions, alterations in the effective mass and density of free electrons, and variations in the crystalline size after the formation of HEAs.

AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

FeCoNiCuAl high-entropy alloys exhibit remarkable mechanical properties; nevertheless, these materials struggle to withstand harsh environments because of their insufficient resistance to wear and corrosion. The addition of Si can significantly enhance the alloy’s high-temperature performance, hardness, and wear resistance, thereby making it more suitable for applications in high-temperature or corrosive environments. To overcome these drawbacks, this research investigates how varying Si content affects the microstructure and properties of FeCoNiCuAl coatings. Composite coatings of FeCoNiCuAlSix (x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0) were fabricated on 65 Mn substrates using laser cladding. Various testing methods, including metallographic microscopy, Vickers hardness testing, friction and wear testing, and electrochemical analysis, were employed to examine the phase structure, microstructure, and hardness of the coating. frame.system: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy in its as-processed state (exhibiting a complex eutectic microstructure with distinct phases ideally suited for both wear resistance and corrosion stability).
frame.goal: To establish a single mechanistic explanation that accounts for the observed accelerated degradation when wear and corrosion occur simultaneously at elevated temperature, and to quantitatively predict the changes in overall degradation and in the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a suitable, well-matched baseline.
frame.limitation: The current inability to explain why the coupling of wear and corrosion under high temperature results in degradation rates that exceed the sum of the individual processes, indicating a gap in understanding the interaction mechanisms between mechanical and chemical degradation in these alloys.
constraints: Must propose a single mechanistic hypothesis
Provide a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation
Predict changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline
frame.regime: Simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosion at elevated temperature (the thermal regime that may accelerate chemical kinetics and alter phase interactions in the alloy).
prior_attempts: Prior studies have separately investigated wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys but have failed to mechanistically integrate the synergistic effects observed when both degradation modes are combined under high temperature.
Controlled experiments that isolated wear and corrosion individually did not account for the interaction effects, leaving an incomplete picture of the degradation process.
